title: Verses of trust (Isaiah 12:2)
hookLine: Havdalah opens with "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust"

lines: A BRAIDED CANDLE, A FULL CUP.
cards: Saturday night. Three stars are out. Somewhere a family is standing in a dim kitchen.
Someone holds a braided candle with several wicks, burning like a small torch. A cup of wine is filled to the brim, spilling over a little onto the plate. A box of spices is passed from hand to hand.
This is Havdalah, separation, the short ceremony that ends Shabbat. And before any blessing is said, before the wine or the fire, the first thing the family says is a line about not being afraid.

teach.h: I WILL TRUST, AND NOT BE AFRAID.
teach.b: Havdalah begins with a handful of verses, mostly from Isaiah and the Psalms. The first, in the old Jewish translation, is Isaiah 12: "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid."
And the next: "Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation." Why start the end of Shabbat with trust? Think about what's happening.
For a day, there were no requests, no work, no money, no errands. Shabbat was a shelter.

teach.h: SO MAY IT BE FOR US.
teach.b: Now the week is about to come back, with everything it carries. So before you step out, you say: I will trust, and will not be afraid.
Then a few more verses of the same kind, and the last one is from the book of Esther, about a moment when danger turned to rescue: "The Jews had light and gladness, and joy and honour."
At that line, in many homes, everyone says together: so may it be for us. Then the four blessings. Over the wine.
Over the spices: tradition says each person is given an extra soul on Shabbat, the one we met in V'shamru, and the fragrance comforts us as it leaves.
Over the fire, the first light kindled after Shabbat, which a midrash connects to Adam, who discovered fire as the very first Shabbat ended.
And then the blessing of separation itself: blessed is the one who separates holy from ordinary, light from darkness, the seventh day from the six days of work. The week begins.
But it begins with trust said first.

how: Havdalah is said after nightfall on Saturday, at home or in synagogue: opening verses of trust, then blessings over wine, fragrant spices and a multi-wicked candle, and the blessing of separation; everyone joins in the line from Esther and responds 'so may it be for us'.

games.q: Shabbat is ending. the week, with all its worries, is about to return. what does Havdalah say first?
o: a list of the week's tasks.
Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid.
games.why: it opens with Isaiah 12:2: trust said first, before wine, spices and fire.

practice: Name to yourself the one thing in the week ahead you're most nervous about. Then say, slowly, aloud or inside: I will trust, and will not be afraid. You don't have to feel it fully; Havdalah says it first, as a way to begin.
